source.title: Concept Concentration for Faithful Representation Intervention
source.authors: Hongzheng Yang; Yong-Qiang Chen; Ze-Yu Qin; Tong-Liang Liu; Chao-Wei Xiao; Kun Zhang; Bo Han

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present. Some table text is flattened, but the Completion Attack and GCG values used below are legible.
record.tranche_reason: Evaluates harmful-compliance rates under jailbreak attacks, including GCG and Completion Attack, which bear on the bypass-by-suffix or affirmative-opening part of V4. It does not test the original studies' token-position KL measurement or a controlled prefill intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper fine-tunes models on mixed safety and helpful data and reports attack success rates, but does not test whether harmful-only or benign-only fine-tuning erodes refusal. It does not measure per-token KL, safety localization in a few weights, or the effect of a controlled compliant prefill or decoding change. For V4, the rows below use the reported GCG and Completion Attack results; other attack categories are not specific tests of suffixes or affirmative openings.
record.test_reason: A defense paper whose baselines bear weakly on V4. Base LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B are safety-tuned through ReFT/LoFiT adapters, then hit with GCG suffixes (Table 9) and a user-turn Completion Attack (Table 1). The vanilla-data arms show how often suffix attacks bypass refusal in this new setting. There is no assistant-turn prefill, no decoding change, and no token-position analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue, theoretically and empirically, that representation interventions such as ReFT and LoFiT fail against OOD jailbreaks when harmful and benign concepts are non-linearly entangled. COCA's structured concept-reasoning data concentrates harmful concepts into a linear subspace, cutting OOD jailbreak ASR while keeping math and code performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates COCA-structured safety fine-tuning and representation interventions against jailbreak attacks. It does not reproduce the original token-position KL or compliant-prefill experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with training data structure (vanilla versus COCA-enhanced) and intervention method (ReFT versus LoFiT); the reported GCG results also differ by method and training-data condition.

fits_no_version.finding: COCA raises the linear-probe max AUC for unsafe-vs-benign prompts (e.g. LLaMA from 0.894 to 0.972). PCA shows harmful and benign representations separating.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety training data structure shapes the linear separability of harmful concepts in representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Code Attack stays high: 83.0/77.0 for vanilla models and 48.0/36.0 with COCA on LLaMA (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Obfuscated harmful intent bypasses refusal training largely independently of the opening tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: For the targeted attacks, the paper reports no uncertainty estimates. GCG values in Table 9 are given without a percent sign. The reported attacks do not isolate the causal effect of passing the first response tokens.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack categories and general ID/OOD ASR results in Tables 1, 5, 7, and 10 are omitted because they are not specifically identified as GCG suffix or Completion Attack tests; helpfulness results and unrelated representation analyses are also omitted.

untested.parts: No benign-only fine-tuning measured for safety erosion.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No assistant-turn prefill or decoding-parameter attacks. The Completion Attack places the compliant opening in the user turn.
No test of safety localized in few weights or ranks.
No test of why alignment is shallow.
COCA puts a reasoning trace before the refusal, but depth of safety beyond the first tokens is never measured.

missing.what: Completion Attack ASR is 0.0 for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, Gemini-1.5 and DeepSeek-R1. These are standard safety-trained models, so the affirmative-completion attack fails on them.
Completion Attack ASR for Qwen-2.5-3B/14B Instruct and for the Gemma-2-9B and Mistral vanilla/enhanced LoFiT arms.
Completion Attack on Circuit Breaker (RR) and CAST/ACE baselines.

record.verdict_notes: The reader misread Table 1's flattened columns: every Completion Attack value recorded was actually the Code Attack value. After correction, Completion Attack is weak against these models, and 0.0 against the Instruct and proprietary models. Completion Attack is a user-turn prompt, so it is only a loose proxy for V4's prefill. GCG is the cleaner V4 evidence, but it appears only for LLaMA in Table 9, with no uncertainty reported. Subjects are base models safety-tuned via adapters, not standard aligned chat models.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples causes harmful compliance.
Does not isolate ordinary or carefully chosen benign-only fine-tuning and measure its effect on harmful compliance.
Does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL across response positions.
Tests GCG and Completion Attack outcomes, but not a controlled compliant-token prefill or decoding changes; it does not establish that bypass works by getting past the first response tokens.
Does not test whether a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether the data or objective causes safety to be shallow in the first response tokens.
COCA changes training data structure and evaluates jailbreak robustness, but the paper does not test whether safety is spread beyond the first tokens or whether such depth holds up.
